title: Revising maths vs essay subjects
examples: Should I just re-read my notes for history?
Is doing practice questions better than writing practice essays?
How do I balance studying different types of subjects?

explain.say: Today we look at studying maths and essay subjects.
For maths, you must practice solving problems often.
For essays, you need to build strong arguments with evidence.
A good plan helps you structure both maths and essays.
In real life, planning helps you manage big projects.
A common mistake is only reading notes for essays.

items: You must write out key ideas.

faq.q: Should I spend equal time on maths and essays?
faq.a: No, you should spend time based on what you find hardest or what the exam weighs more heavily. You might need more practice time for one subject than the other.
asks: How do I decide where to focus my study time?
Is it better to study everything a little bit?

faq.q: When should I start planning my revision?
faq.a: You should start planning as soon as you know the exam topics. A good plan breaks the whole subject into smaller, manageable chunks.
asks: Do I need a plan for every single subject?
Can I plan my revision last minute?

faq.q: Does 'practice' mean doing problems or writing answers?
faq.a: For maths, practice means doing problems. For essays, practice means writing full answers, not just thinking about them.
asks: What is the difference between thinking and doing?
Is writing a practice essay the same as writing for a grade?

faq.q: Can I use quotes to help me study maths?
faq.a: Quotes are useful for subjects like literature or history. For maths, your evidence should be solved examples or formulas, not famous sayings.
asks: Are quotes good for all subjects?
Where do I find evidence for maths?

faq.q: If I plan my revision, what should I do next?
faq.a: After planning, you should actively study the first topic. Then, you should review your plan to see if you need to adjust your focus.
asks: What comes after making a study schedule?
Should I revise the plan after I study?

facts: Maths requires consistent application of skills through practice.
Essay writing requires developing a clear, supported argument.
A study plan helps break large amounts of work into smaller steps.
Active recall, like explaining concepts aloud, is highly effective for both types of subjects.

quiz.say: To revise for a maths test, which activity is most effective?
quiz.why: Maths skills are built by doing, so repeated practice is key.

wrong.0: Reading is passive and does not build the necessary problem-solving muscle.
wrong.1: Watching is good, but you must pause and try the problem yourself afterward.
wrong.2: While useful, definitions alone do not test your ability to use the concept.

quiz.say: When revising for an essay, what is the most important step after outlining your points?
quiz.why: An essay needs more than just ideas; it needs proof and analysis to back up those ideas.

wrong.0: While refining is good, spending too much time on the start neglects the main body.
wrong.1: This is important, but it comes after you have written the core argument.
wrong.3: Quotes are good for some subjects, but they are not the evidence for an argument.

quiz.say: If you are planning revision for both subjects, what should your plan emphasize?

options.show: Spending all time on the hardest subject
options.say: Spending all time on the hardest subject

options.show: Only revising topics you enjoy most
options.say: Only revising topics you enjoy most

quiz.why: You need structured plans for essays and dedicated practice time for maths.

wrong.0: A good plan needs regular checking and adjustment as you learn more.
wrong.2: This can lead to burnout and neglecting necessary foundational knowledge.
wrong.3: You must cover all required topics, even the ones you find difficult.
